holidays.name: National Deviled Egg Day
holidays.description: A day to celebrate the humble party-platter classic: hard-boiled egg whites filled with a creamy, tangy yolk mixture. Dust them with paprika, top them with bacon, or go wild with sriracha. Today, anything goes.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial food observance of unclear origin. It has become a fixture on the calendar of quirky food days.
holidays.funFact: The name comes from the old practice of calling spicy or zesty foods 'deviled.' The term was in use by the 18th century, and the dish itself dates back to ancient Rome, where boiled eggs were served with spicy sauces.

holidays.name: Look for Circles Day
holidays.description: An invitation to slow down and spot circles hiding in plain sight, such as clocks, wheels, coins, manhole covers, bubbles and the bottoms of coffee mugs. Once you start looking, you'll see them everywhere.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It is a playful nudge to notice the shapes in everyday life.
holidays.funFact: Circles are everywhere in nature. Ripples in a pond, the pupils of your eyes, and the shape of the Sun and Moon in our sky all follow the pattern. Ancient cultures treated the circle as a symbol of eternity and unity.

holidays.name: Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead) and All Souls' Day
holidays.description: In Mexico and many other places, November 2 is the day families remember their departed loved ones. They build colorful ofrendas (altars) piled with marigolds, sugar skulls, candles, photos and the favorite foods of those who have died. It is a joyful, affectionate celebration of life and memory rather than a gloomy occasion.
holidays.origin: The tradition blends Indigenous Aztec practices honoring the dead with the Catholic observance of All Souls' Day. Celebrations traditionally run from November 1 to 2. November 1 honors children and November 2 honors adults.
holidays.funFact: UNESCO added Mexico's Day of the Dead to its Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2008. Marigolds, called cempasúchil, are believed to guide spirits home with their bright color and strong scent.
